title: Opinions with reasons
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: anna is "that", and what comes straight after it is a NOUN or a pronoun welded to its back — never a verb. aʿtaqid anna al-ʿarabiyya jamīla, aʿtaqid annahā ṣaʿba, aẓunn anna hind dhahabat. English's "that" holds anything and can even be dropped; anna holds one thing and is never dropped.

The reason is the ACCUSATIVE: anna and its sisters put the noun after them in that case. This course writes no case endings, so a definite noun looks unchanged on the page — L3-M1 said the same of the genitive. What you CAN see is the pronoun: the accusative is why it has to attach, so annahā and annahu are the case made visible, and anna hiya does not exist. That single cell is all of the case system this module opens.

li-ʾanna is that same anna with L1-M9's li- glued on the front, and it keeps the identical habit: a noun or an attached pronoun behind it, never a bare verb — li-ʾanna al-ḥisāb ghālī, li-ʾannahu ghālī. One rule buys both words, and L1-M9 already paid for the second.

aʿtaqid and aẓunn are ordinary imperfect verbs on L1-M4's prefix law, with no ending on them, and both hand their clause to anna. The negative is L1-M3's lā in front of the verb — lā aʿtaqid anna hādhā ṣaḥīḥ — and the clause behind anna does not change at all.

Softening in Arabic is a FRAME in front of the sentence, not a weakening inside it. fī raʾyī (L1-M9), rubbamā and lā aʿtaqid stand outside the claim and leave it whole. English hedges inside — "it's sort of right", "it might be a bit hard" — and doing that in Arabic sounds evasive rather than careful. Neither language is being polite better; they put the politeness in different places.

Agreeing is an ADJECTIVE, not a verb: anā muwāfiq (L2-M6), muwāfiqa from a woman. Its negative is L2-M7's laysa in the first person, lastu muwāfiq, because a verbless sentence cannot be denied with lā. Nothing after lastu takes an ending here, exactly as L2-M7 wrote huwa laysa mawjūd.

The comparison an opinion reaches for is already yours. jayyid and sayyiʾ are new, but akbar, aghlā, arkhaṣ and the whole afʿal shape are L2-M9's and min is L1-M1's third job. This module adds no comparative and needs none.

words.note: "I think" — an ordinary imperfect verb on L1-M4's a- prefix, with no ending on the end of it. What it thinks is handed to anna, never straight to a verb.
"That" — and a noun or an attached pronoun has to come next: anna al-ʿarabiyya, annahā. English's "that" can hold a verb and can be dropped; anna can do neither.

sentences.trap: English drops "that" — I think Arabic is beautiful. Arabic cannot: anna is what carries the clause, and aʿtaqid al-ʿarabiyya jamīla is not a sentence at all.
sentences.sound: aʿ-TA-qid AN-na al-ʿa-ra-BEE-ya — the n of anna is held doubled, and the ʿ in aʿtaqid is the throat-squeeze of L1-M4's ʿamal.

variations.cue: I think the coffee is delicious
variations.changed: what is being judged: the language becomes the coffee

variations.cue: I think the book is excellent
variations.changed: a masculine noun after anna, so the adjective loses its -a

mistake.why: English can leave "that" out, so an English speaker leaves anna out too. Arabic then has nothing holding the clause: aʿtaqid anna al-ʿarabiyya jamīla.

sentences.usage: The plainest way to give an opinion in Arabic, and the frame the rest of the module hangs on.
sentences.mnemonic: anna is the hinge; the door will not swing without it.

sentences.cue: I think it's difficult, but important

words.note: anna with the pronoun welded to its back: annahā (she, it-f), annahu (he, it-m), annaka (you-m), annaki (you-f). anna hiya does not exist — the pronoun must attach.

sentences.trap: The pronoun cannot stand free after anna. English says "that it is difficult" in separate words; Arabic welds the pronoun on and leaves no gap to put one in.
sentences.sound: an-na-HAA — the n is held doubled in the middle and the -hā runs long off the end; that tail is where the sentence's subject is hiding.

variations.cue: I think he is busy today
variations.changed: the attached pronoun: -hā (she) becomes -hu (he)

variations.cue: I think you are an excellent teacher (to a man)
variations.changed: the pronoun turns to face the listener: -ka

mistake.why: English keeps its pronoun as its own word and this copies it across. anna will not hold a free pronoun, only a suffixed one: aʿtaqid annahā ṣaʿba.

sentences.usage: How a second thing is said about something already named, without naming it again.
sentences.mnemonic: anna never stands beside a free pronoun; it wears it.

sentences.cue: In my opinion, that's completely right

words.note: "Right" — ṣaḥīḥ of a masculine thing, ṣaḥīḥa of a feminine one. Heavy ṣ at the front and the breathy ḥ of ṣabāḥ in the middle.
"Completely" — the written -an of shukran and jiddan, the adverbial tail L3-M1's rule 3 named. It follows whatever it strengthens: ṣaḥīḥ tamāman.

sentences.trap: fī raʾyī is not a verb and adds none — L1-M9 already said so. It changes the claim's standing, not its grammar: what follows the comma is the same verbless sentence.
sentences.sound: fee RAʾ-yee, HAA-dhaa ṣa-ḤEEḤ ta-MAA-man — the catch in raʾyī is audible between its syllables, and tamāman ends on the -an you can hear.

variations.cue: In my opinion, that's right
variations.changed: tamāman dropped — the same claim, only quieter

variations.cue: That is completely right
variations.changed: the softener taken off the front, leaving the bare claim

mistake.why: hādhā is masculine, so its adjective is ṣaḥīḥ. The -a is the feminine ending and here it agrees with nothing: fī raʾyī, hādhā ṣaḥīḥ.

sentences.usage: The everyday way to agree with something just said, with fī raʾyī marking it as yours rather than as fact.
sentences.mnemonic: tamāman is the full stop you can hear.

sentences.cue: This is a very good idea

words.note: "Idea" — feminine, so its adjectives take -a: fikra jayyida. Its plural afkār is broken and comes with the word, the way L3-M2's rawātib did.
"Good" — jayyid of a masculine thing, jayyida of a feminine one. fikra is feminine, hence the -a. Its opposite, sayyiʾ, turns up later in the module.

sentences.trap: "A very good idea" needs no "is" and no "a" in Arabic. hādhihi fikra jayyida is already a whole sentence, three words long.
sentences.sound: HAA-dhi-hi FIK-ra JAY-yi-da JID-dan — the doubled y in jayyida is held, and holding it is the only thing that separates it from a word with one.

variations.cue: This is a good idea, but an expensive one
variations.changed: a second judgement hung on L1-M10's lākin

variations.cue: This is a very good book
variations.changed: a masculine noun, so jayyida loses its -a

mistake.why: English has one form of "good" and Arabic has two. fikra is feminine, so the adjective has to be as well: hādhihi fikra jayyida.

sentences.usage: What you say when somebody proposes something — the shortest approval in the module.
sentences.mnemonic: A feminine idea takes a feminine good.

sentences.display: lastu muwāfiq, li-ʾanna hādhā ghālī jiddan
sentences.script: لست موافق، لأن هذا غالي جدًا
sentences.cue: I don't agree, because this is very expensive
sentences.literal: I-am-not agreeing, because this expensive very

words.note: The first person of L2-M7's laysa, the negative a verbless sentence needs: lastu muwāfiq. laysa is he, laysat is she, and what follows takes no ending.

sentences.trap: lā will not do this job. lā denies a VERB, and anā muwāfiq has none — the sentence needs laysa, and its first person is lastu.
sentences.sound: LAS-tu mu-WAA-fiq — lastu is one clipped syllable and a stop, and it does not lean on what comes after it.

variations.cue: I don't agree, because I'm busy
variations.changed: the reason turns personal: li-ʾanna takes L1-M9's attached -ī

variations.cue: I agree, because this is cheap
variations.changed: the whole stance flips and lastu goes back to anā

mistake.why: lā is the negative for a verb, and muwāfiq is an adjective. A verbless sentence is denied with laysa, whose first person is lastu: lastu muwāfiq.

sentences.usage: Disagreeing without being rude — the reason hung on li-ʾanna is what keeps it civil.
sentences.mnemonic: lā for doing, lastu for being.

sentences.display: rubbamā, lākin fī raʾyī hādhā ṣaʿb
sentences.script: ربما، لكن في رأيي هذا صعب
sentences.cue: Maybe, but in my opinion this is hard
sentences.literal: Perhaps, but in opinion-my this difficult

words.note: "Perhaps" — one word standing in front of what it doubts and bending nothing behind it: rubbamā yadhhab ghadan. It is not a verb and carries no person.

sentences.trap: English hedges inside the claim — it's kind of hard, it might be hard. Arabic puts the hedge outside it: rubbamā and fī raʾyī stand in front and leave the sentence whole.
sentences.sound: RUB-ba-maa — the b is doubled and held, then a long -mā runs off the end of it.

variations.cue: Perhaps he'll go to the market tomorrow
variations.changed: rubbamā in front of a verb, where it still bends nothing

variations.cue: Maybe, but I don't agree
variations.changed: the second half becomes a flat disagreement

mistake.why: English stacks its hedges — I think maybe it's hard. Arabic does not: aʿtaqid hands its clause to anna and rubbamā cannot stand between them. Pick one — rubbamā hādhā ṣaʿb, or aʿtaqid annahu ṣaʿb.

sentences.usage: The polite half-agreement: you concede the point and keep your own, which is the work lākin is doing in the middle.
sentences.mnemonic: rubbamā leans on nothing; it just stands in front.

sentences.cue: I think this is a big mistake

words.note: "A mistake" — a noun, so "a big mistake" is khaṭaʾ kabīr with L1-M3's adjective behind it. It ends on a written hamza, heard as a catch: khaṭaʾ, not khaṭā.

sentences.trap: hādhā is what stands after anna here and it does not change shape for anything. The accusative anna imposes is invisible on a demonstrative — which is why rule 2 states it on the attached pronoun, where it can be seen.
sentences.sound: kha-ṬAʾ ka-BEER — the throaty kh at the front, and the word stops dead on the hamza instead of trailing off into a long vowel.

variations.cue: I think this is a mistake
variations.changed: kabīr dropped — the judgement stands without its size

variations.cue: In my opinion, this is a big mistake
variations.changed: the frame: aʿtaqid anna becomes fī raʾyī, and the clause stops needing anna

mistake.why: English puts anything behind "that", a verb included. anna cannot hold one — what follows it is a noun or an attached pronoun: aʿtaqid anna hādhā khaṭaʾ kabīr.

sentences.usage: The strongest disagreement the module teaches, and it names the thing rather than the person.
sentences.mnemonic: khaṭaʾ ends on a catch — the sound of stopping short.

sentences.display: aẓunn anna hind dhahabat ilā as-sūq
sentences.script: أظن أن هند ذهبت إلى السوق
sentences.cue: I think Hind went to the market
sentences.literal: I-suppose that Hind went(f) to the-market

words.note: "I suppose" — aʿtaqid's everyday twin, and one of anna's sisters in the same way: it hands its clause to anna. The ẓ is the heavy one, said with the tongue flat.

sentences.trap: An ordinary Arabic sentence may start with its verb — dhahabat hind. Behind anna it may not: the noun comes first, because the noun is what anna is holding.
sentences.sound: a-ẒUNN — the ẓ is heavy and the n is doubled, so the word ends on a hum rather than a stop.

variations.cue: I think Hind is an excellent teacher
variations.changed: a verbless clause behind anna instead of a past one

variations.display: aʿtaqid anna hind dhahabat ilā al-madrasa
variations.script: أعتقد أن هند ذهبت إلى المدرسة
variations.cue: I think Hind went to the school
variations.changed: aẓunn swapped for aʿtaqid, which changes nothing else

mistake.display: aẓunn anna dhahabat hind ilā as-sūq
mistake.script: أظن أن ذهبت هند إلى السوق
mistake.why: Arabic's plain sentence can put the verb first — dhahabat hind — and a learner who has met that order tries it here. Behind anna the noun leads: anna hind dhahabat.

sentences.usage: How you report what you believe about someone else without claiming to know it.
sentences.mnemonic: anna wants a name before it wants a deed.

sentences.display: fī raʾyī, al-maṭʿam sayyiʾ li-ʾanna al-ḥisāb ghālī
sentences.script: في رأيي، المطعم سيئ لأن الحساب غالي
sentences.cue: In my opinion the restaurant is bad, because the bill is expensive
sentences.literal: In opinion-my, the-restaurant bad because the-bill expensive

words.note: "Bad" — sayyiʾ of a masculine thing, sayyiʾa of a feminine one, and the plain opposite of jayyid. The hamza at its end is a catch, not a long vowel.

sentences.trap: li-ʾanna is L1-M9's word and it behaves here exactly as it did there — a noun or an attached pronoun behind it, never a bare verb. anna and li-ʾanna are one particle with one habit.
sentences.sound: SAY-yiʾ — the doubled y is held and the word stops on the hamza; li-ʾAN-na al-ḥi-SAAB then runs on with no pause in it.

variations.display: fī raʾyī, al-maṭʿam sayyiʾ li-ʾannahu ghālī
variations.script: في رأيي، المطعم سيئ لأنه غالي
variations.cue: In my opinion the restaurant is bad, because it's expensive
variations.changed: the reason's noun becomes an attached pronoun: -hu

variations.cue: The restaurant is excellent, because the bill is cheap
variations.changed: both judgements flip and the frame does not move

mistake.display: fī raʾyī, al-maṭʿam sayyiʾ li-ʾanna ghālī
mistake.script: في رأيي، المطعم سيئ لأن غالي
mistake.why: English puts "because" straight in front of anything, a bare adjective included. li-ʾanna needs a noun or an attached pronoun first: li-ʾanna al-ḥisāb ghālī, or li-ʾannahu ghālī.

sentences.usage: An opinion with its reason attached is the module's whole job, and this is the longest version of it.
sentences.mnemonic: li-ʾanna is anna wearing L1-M9's li-.

words.note: L1-M3's lā in front of the verb, exactly where English puts its "don't". The clause behind anna is left untouched by it: lā aʿtaqid anna hādhā ṣaḥīḥ.

sentences.trap: Nothing behind anna moves when the front of the sentence is negated — no second lā, no different form. English behaves the same way, and this is one of the places the two languages agree.
sentences.sound: laa aʿ-TA-qid — the lā is short and leans straight onto the verb, with the ʿayn squeezed in behind it.

variations.cue: I don't think the exam is easy
variations.changed: what is doubted: a claim about something L3-M2 already taught

variations.cue: I don't suppose that's right
variations.changed: aʿtaqid swapped for aẓunn, which the lā treats identically

mistake.why: The negative belongs on the verb, not in front of anna. Arabic denies the thinking and leaves the thought alone: lā aʿtaqid anna hādhā ṣaḥīḥ.

sentences.usage: The softest disagreement in the module — it doubts the claim rather than contradicting the person.
sentences.mnemonic: Deny the thinking, not the thought.

comprehensionPool.cue: I think the coffee is delicious
In my opinion, this book is excellent
I don't agree, because the weather is cold
Perhaps he'll go to school tomorrow
I think he is busy today
I think the restaurant is very expensive
I don't think the exam is easy
In my opinion the music is very lovely
I think Hind is an excellent student
That's a big mistake, in my opinion
